text: About 10,000 years ago, the ancestors of the San lived from Tanzania all the way to the south of Africa.
The San have no single name for themselves, but use their nations’ names, such as ǃKung, ǀXam and Khwe.
src: Some 10,000 years ago such groups were spread from Tanzania, Zambia and Angola down to Cape Agulhas / There is a general consensus that the modern San descend from the oldest societies of southern and eastern Africa
They have no collective word for themselves: they use the names of their own nations, such as the ǃKung (including the Juǀʼhoansi), ǀXam, Nǁnǂe, Khwe

text: For thousands of years they moved with the seasons, following water, animals and plants.
Men hunted with bows and poisoned arrows, women gathered fruit and roots, and people shared through gifts.
src: The San were traditionally semi-nomadic, moving with the seasons within defined areas according to water, game and edible plants

Men, and sometimes women, hunted on long tracking trips with bows, arrows and spears tipped with diamphotoxin, a slow-acting poison / Women gathered fruit, berries, tubers and bush onions / The economy was a gift economy, built on regular giving rather than trade

text: San painters left pictures on rocks across southern Africa, showing hunting, daily life and stories.
San shamans, people who deal with the spirit world, went into a trance to bring rain.
src: Early San societies left a rich legacy of paintings on rock across southern Africa, showing hunting, battles, domestic life and mythological events
San shamans entered a trance and went into the spirit world themselves to capture the animals associated with rain / turned to them for rainmaking

text: From about 1714, Dutch stock farmers called Trekboers moved into San lands and took their waterholes.
Their armed groups killed thousands of San, and many others were forced to work on farms.
src: From about 1714 the Dutch East India Company’s loan farms sent Trekboer stock farmers into San lands, where they took the waterholes
From the 18th century Dutch colonists’ commandos killed thousands of San at the Cape / By the 1850s most San had been tied to farmers by threats, the holding of wives and children, and starvation

text: Today many San live in Botswana and Namibia, and they work together to defend their rights and their land.
In 2003 they won an agreement to be paid for their knowledge of a plant called hoodia.
src: about 63,500 San in Botswana (2017) and 71,201 in Namibia (2023) / The San have organised to defend their rights / they still contend for land and recognition
in 2003 the San won a benefit-sharing agreement with South Africa’s CSIR over the hoodia plant, one of the first to pay royalties to the holders of traditional knowledge
